title: KV cache — host PCIe/UMA paging thresholds and runtime policy (draft)
content:
Summary:
This is a working draft of a host-driven KV cache paging and offload policy targeting discrete-GPU and UMA-style platforms. It proposes: (1) a lightweight host paging controller that coordinates PCIe DMA transfers and host-memory page residency, (2) heuristics and measurable thresholds for when to evict/restore KV pages, and (3) runtime hooks into the request scheduler to prioritize transfers and avoid latency cliffs. The goal is to reduce GPU memory pressure for large-context workloads while bounding tail latency impact and keeping operational observability simple.

Motivation and constraints:
- Common workloads: many concurrent chat sessions share base KV prefix; during long-context generations KV cache can exceed device RAM.
- Platforms: (A) discrete GPU (separate CPU DRAM + GPU VRAM over PCIe) and (B) UMA platforms (e.g., integrated accelerators or APUs where CPU/GPU share physical memory). We must support both with a single control plane but different low-level implementations.
- Constraints: PCIe bandwidth is limited and high-latency compared to on-card accesses. Paging decisions must avoid introducing long token-level stalls. Eviction/restore operations should be non-blocking for latency-sensitive requests where possible.

Design overview:
1) Two-tier residency model:
   - Resident: pages pinned in GPU-local memory (fastest).
   - Staged: pages resident in host DRAM but pinned for DMA (fast restore via async PCIe transfer).
   - Cold: pages not pinned and possibly swapped to disk or left as compact protobuf on host (slow restore).
   Implementation note: on UMA, Resident/Staged map to the same physical memory; controller simplifies to tracking "logical residency" and avoiding copies.

2) Host paging controller (HPC) responsibilities:
   - Maintain per-model and per-shard LRU-ish index for KV pages with age/access frequency metrics.
   - Expose async APIs to scheduler: request_page_async(page_id, priority) and cancel_request(page_id).
   - Coalesce nearby page restores into bulk DMA when PCIe efficiency suggests (batch size heuristic below).
   - Track ongoing PCIe transfer budgets to avoid saturating host<->device link and degrading RPC/ingress paths.

3) Scheduler integration and request prioritization:
   - Each inference request is tagged with a latency priority (SLO-critical | best-effort | background).
   - On cache miss, scheduler queries HPC. If page is Staged or Resident: cheap. If Cold: scheduler decides whether to: (a) wait for restore (within a timeout), (b) fall back to smaller-model/compressed path, or (c) return degraded output.
   - For SLO-critical requests, we favor preemption of background transfers and immediate single-page restore (low-latency single-DMA path). For background, prefer coalesced bulk restores.

4) Heuristics and thresholds (initial recommended defaults):
   - Warm-up threshold: if a page is accessed >= 3 times within window T=2s, mark as hot and ensure Resident or Staged depending on free VRAM.
   - Resident promotion: promote Staged->Resident when free VRAM fraction > 0.15 and predicted next-token access prob > 0.6 (EWMAs maintained per-page).
   - Eviction policy: evict pages with access_rate < 0.1 ops/s and age > 30s when VRAM pressure > 0.75.
   - PCIe coalesce threshold: if >4 distinct adjacent pages requested within 10ms, issue a single bulk DMA for contiguous region (reduces per-transfer overhead).
   - PCIe backpressure cap: limit HPC-initiated bandwidth to 60% of measured link throughput in last 1s to leave headroom for other system traffic.
   - Max restore latency budget per request: SLO-critical requests get budget 20ms for restore; if budget exceeded, fallback is triggered.

5) UMA vs discrete specifics:
   - UMA: avoid copies whenever page is readable from both CPU and accelerator; residency is logical flags and pinning is no-op. Prefetch still useful to avoid TLB misses and warm caches.
   - Discrete: implement pinned host pages in host DRAM to support fast DMA; fallback cold pages may be compressed on disk.
   - For NVMe-backed swap: use async IO and maintain small working set on host pinned memory to limit NVMe->DRAM stalls.

6) Eviction and reclaim strategies:
   - Lazy eviction: mark page evictable and start async write-out (if dirty) while scheduler prefers other pages; actual free occurs only after bandwidth budget check passes.
   - Quick-reclaim fence: if reclaiming page would free <1.5x the anticipated immediate demand, skip reclaim to avoid churn.

7) Prefetching and prediction:
   - Sequence-based prefetching: for model families with predictable KV traversal patterns (e.g., autoregressive with sliding windows), prefetch next N pages ahead when generating long contexts.
   - Model-profiled heuristics: during onboarding, run a short sampler to record access stride patterns to seed prefetch rules. These profiles are stored as metadata and can be versioned per-model.

8) Observability and metrics (must include):
   - per-model: resident_pages, staged_pages, cold_pages, evictions/sec, restores/sec, avg_restore_latency, p99_restore_latency, pci_bandwidth_used_pct.
   - per-request: restore_wait_time, fallback_triggered, pages_restored.
   - alerts: p99_restore_latency > 50ms or pci_bandwidth_used_pct > 80% for >30s.

9) Safety nets and fallbacks:
   - Always expose a "degraded path" model variant that is smaller and fully resident on GPU to serve when restore budgets are exhausted.
   - Safety throttle: if cumulative restore wait time in the last 1s across requests exceeds threshold, refuse new Staged->Resident promotions until metric recovers.

10) Rollout plan (staged):
   - Phase 0: telemetry-only (collect access patterns and link metrics) deployed in staging clusters for 2 weeks.
   - Phase 1: enable Staged residency with conservative thresholds (Resident promotion threshold 0.3 free VRAM, backpressure cap 40%). Enable only for non-critical traffic for 1 week.
   - Phase 2: enable SLO-priority fast-path restores and coalesced bulk transfers; run A/B to compare p99 tail latency and token-cost impacts.
   - Phase 3: enable UMA shortcuts and NVMe-backed swap for large-batch tenants, with opt-in via tenant config.

Open questions and engineering tasks (short):
- Pinning model: which OS-level allocators and kernel flags to use for cross-platform pinned pages (linux: mlock/memfd or CUDA IPC?). Need a prototype that measures mlock costs vs cudaHostAlloc for pinned pages.
- Consistency: when pages are dirty due to KV updates during generation, define write-back protocol and ordering guarantees.
- Scheduler API: finalize the async request_page_async API shape and priority enums; decide whether HPC runs in-process or as separate daemon.
- Profiling harness: small benchmark to exercise random and sliding-window access at scale to calibrate thresholds.

Appendix: quick estimation notes
- PCIe Gen3 x16 practical throughput ~11GB/s, Gen4 x16 ~28GB/s. A single 256KB page transfer is ~0.02ms at Gen4 peak but practical latencies + DMA setup push to ~0.5–2ms for small transfers. This motivates coalescing and batch restores for throughput efficiency.
- For a model with 1M KV tokens split into 64KB pages, worst-case cold restore of 16 pages (~1MB) likely costs ~1–5ms on Gen4 if coalesced, but per-page latency without coalesce can be 0.5–2ms each leading to unacceptable tail.

Requested next steps:
- Engineering: implement minimal HPC prototype with two modes (single-page low-latency DMA and bulk coalesced DMA) and a simple scheduler hook.
- Research: run microbenchmarks on our smallest and largest supported instance families to collect real restore latencies and PCIe saturation behavior.
- Product: validate the fallback UX and per-tenant opt-ins for UMA vs discrete strategies.

Notes-to-self / TODOs (work-in-progress):
- Add sequence diagrams showing request->scheduler->HPC->DMA->resume flow.
- Draft kube operator knobs for resident fraction and bandwidth cap per tenant.
- Cross-ref to storage team for NVMe-backed swap file layout and encryption-at-rest requirements.

End of draft.
